one: One thread runs your JS. Work queued for later waits in task queues; the event loop picks it up when the call stack is empty, running all microtasks before the next task.
an: A single cashier. Customers in line are tasks. Promise callbacks are people with "just one quick question": the cashier answers every one of them before calling the next customer, and only redraws the shop sign between customers.
how: The call stack runs synchronous code to completion. Nothing interrupts it.

Tasks (also called macrotasks): setTimeout/setInterval callbacks, I/O callbacks, UI events, MessageChannel messages. Microtasks: promise reactions (.then, the code after await), queueMicrotask, MutationObserver callbacks.

One turn of the browser loop: run one task → drain the entire microtask queue (including microtasks added while draining) → if it is time for a frame, run requestAnimationFrame callbacks, then style, layout and paint → next task.

The microtask queue is also drained every time the call stack becomes empty inside a task. For a real user click, that means between two click listeners on the same element. (If your code calls el.click(), the stack is not empty between listeners, so microtasks wait until all listeners finish.)
So console.log(1); setTimeout(() => log(2)); Promise.resolve().then(() => log(3)); log(4) prints 1, 4, 3, 2.

Node has the same idea with different queues: process.nextTick callbacks run first, then promise microtasks, then the loop moves through its phases (timers, I/O poll, setImmediate “check”, close callbacks).
why: Explains why UIs freeze, why setTimeout(fn, 0) is not immediate, why state updates batch, and a whole category of ordering bugs and interview questions.
trade: A microtask that keeps scheduling microtasks starves rendering forever. Long synchronous work blocks input. Break work up by yielding a real task (scheduler.yield() where supported, otherwise setTimeout), or move it to a worker.

myth.r: It runs after the current task finishes, all microtasks drain, and possibly a render. After 5 levels of nested timers browsers clamp the delay to at least 4ms, and hidden tabs throttle timers much more.

plain:
JavaScript can only do one thing at a time. When something has to wait (a timer, a network reply, a click), the browser puts a note in a waiting line. When the current code is completely finished, the event loop takes the next note from the line and runs it.

There are two lines. Promise callbacks go in the fast lane (microtasks). Timers, clicks and network events go in the normal lane (tasks). After every task, the fast lane is emptied completely before anything else happens, including drawing the screen.
bridge: You see this every day in React. A click handler that sorts a big list makes the whole page freeze until it finishes, because rendering and new clicks wait in line behind your code. And state updates from one handler are batched: React renders once after the handler finishes, not after every setState call.

walk.title: What happens when the user clicks “Save”
steps: The click becomes a task in the normal lane. The loop picks it up and runs your onClick handler.
Your handler sets a “saving” state and calls fetch('/api/save'). The browser starts the network request in the background and immediately gives you a pending promise. Your handler finishes.
The call stack is now empty. The loop empties the fast lane (any promise callbacks waiting). Then, at the next frame, the browser paints the spinner.
About 200ms later, the response arrives. A network task resolves the promise, and the code after await (or your .then) runs as a microtask right after it.
You set new state; React schedules a render; the browser paints the “Saved” message on the next frame.

terms: The list of functions running right now. JS works on the top one until the stack is empty.
A unit of work from the normal lane: a timer callback, a click handler, a network event.
A promise callback or queueMicrotask. Runs before the next task and before painting.
Code that runs so long that nothing else, including clicks and painting, can happen.
insights: “Async” does not mean “in parallel”. It means “later, on the same thread”. Two heavy async functions still freeze the page.
If a page feels frozen, look for one long task in the DevTools Performance panel. It is almost always one function doing too much at once.
Timers are minimums, not appointments. setTimeout(fn, 100) means “not before 100ms”. A busy main thread or a hidden tab can make it run much later.

prod.summary: In production the event loop shows up as slow interactions: a click that takes 400ms to paint, a Node API whose p99 latency jumps when one request parses a big JSON body. Seniors look for long tasks on the main thread (browser) or event-loop delay (Node), and split or move heavy work before users feel it.
checklist: No single task on the main thread runs longer than 50ms on a mid-range phone. Check the DevTools Performance panel with 4x CPU throttling, not your laptop at full speed.
INP (Interaction to Next Paint) from real users is at or below 200ms at p75. Lab tests alone do not show it.
Big loops over data (sorting 50k rows, parsing CSV, diffing) are chunked with scheduler.yield() (feature-detected, with a setTimeout fallback) or moved to a Web Worker / worker_threads.
In Node, synchronous APIs (fs.readFileSync, crypto.pbkdf2Sync, JSON.parse of multi-MB bodies, catastrophic regexes) are not used inside request handlers.
Node services export event-loop delay (perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay) as a metric and alert on its p99.
Recursive queueMicrotask, process.nextTick or promise chains cannot loop forever; they would starve timers, I/O and rendering.
Code does not depend on exact setTimeout timing: timers are minimums, and hidden tabs throttle them heavily.
numbers: A “long task” is any task over 50ms (Long Tasks API, Chrome DevTools red corner marker).
Core Web Vitals: INP is “good” at ≤ 200ms and “poor” above 500ms, measured at the 75th percentile.
A 60Hz screen gives one frame every 16.7ms; work longer than that in one task drops frames.
HTML spec: once timers are nested more than 5 levels deep, a delay below 4ms is clamped to 4ms.
Node: the process.nextTick queue runs before the promise microtask queue, after each callback.
failures: Users report “the button does nothing for a second”; INP p75 in RUM is 650ms on Android.

The click handler filters and sorts a 40k-item array synchronously, then React re-renders the whole list. Fix: virtualise the list, move the filter to a Worker or chunk it with scheduler.yield(), and use useTransition so input stays responsive.
Node API p99 jumps from 40ms to 2s every few minutes; CPU is only 30% on average.

One endpoint does JSON.parse + transform on a 30MB upload, blocking the single thread; every other request waits. Fix: cap body size on purpose (express.json({ limit: '1mb' })), stream-parse large uploads, or move the work to worker_threads or a job queue.
A progress bar never updates during a long import, then jumps to 100%.

The import loop is async but every await resolves immediately (already-resolved promises), so it only yields to microtasks and the browser never gets a chance to paint. Fix: yield a real task (await scheduler.yield() or await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r))) every N items.
A polling dashboard shows data minutes old when the tab was in the background.

Browsers throttle timers in hidden tabs (Chrome: at most once per second, and more heavily after minutes hidden). Fix: refetch on visibilitychange/focus, or use push (SSE/WebSocket) instead of tight setInterval polling.
Health checks time out and Kubernetes restarts healthy-looking Node pods.

Event-loop blocking (a sync bcrypt hash, a huge regex) stops the process from answering /healthz in time. Fix: use async crypto APIs, monitor event-loop delay, and give the liveness probe a realistic timeout.

qs.s: A Node service shows eventLoopDelay p99 = 1.8s while CPU averages 25%. Which explanation fits best?
o: The server needs more CPU cores, because Node uses all of them for JS
The database is slow, so queries are blocking the event loop
Garbage collection always causes multi-second pauses in Node
Some request runs long synchronous code; average CPU is low, but while it runs every other callback waits
qs.e: Event-loop delay measures how late callbacks run. A slow database does not block the loop: the query waits off-thread and the loop stays free. Low average CPU with high loop delay is the classic sign of short bursts of blocking sync work.

qs.s: You split a 2-second loop into chunks with for (...) { work(); await Promise.resolve(); }. The page is still frozen. Why?
o: await inside a for loop is not allowed in browsers
Awaiting a resolved promise only queues a microtask; the browser renders and handles input only between tasks, so nothing can happen until the loop ends
Promise.resolve() is synchronous and does not yield at all
The chunks are too small; they should be bigger
qs.e: Microtasks run before rendering and before the next task. You need a task boundary: scheduler.yield(), setTimeout or MessageChannel. “Promise.resolve() does not yield at all” is close, but the await does yield — just to the microtask queue, which is not enough.

o: Each await on a promise adds about 4ms of microtask overhead
The browser renders a frame (16.7ms) after every setTimeout, so the loop waits for each frame
setTimeout is throttled to once per second in all tabs
After 5 nested timers the browser clamps the delay to at least 4ms, so 10,000 yields cost about 10,000 × 4ms = 40s
qs.e: Each new timer is created from inside the previous timer's task, so the nesting level grows. Past 5 levels, the HTML spec clamps delays to 4ms. Fix: yield only when a time budget (e.g. 40ms) is used up, and prefer scheduler.yield() or a MessageChannel, which are not clamped. Rendering is not forced after each task; the browser paints only when a frame is due.

qs.s: A Node API resizes uploaded images with a pure-JS library. Each resize takes ~300ms of CPU. Under load, all endpoints get slow, even /healthz. Which change actually fixes it?
o: Run the resize in a worker thread pool (e.g. Piscina) or a separate job queue, so the main thread only receives the result
Mark the resize function async and await it
Wrap the call in setImmediate so it runs later
Raise UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE to 64
qs.e: CPU-bound JS blocks the one thread that runs every callback. async and setImmediate only change when the 300ms block happens, not where. The libuv thread pool only runs native work (fs, dns, crypto, zlib); it does not run your JS. A worker thread or a separate service moves the CPU work off the main loop.

interview.q: Walk me through what happens between a user clicking a button and the next frame being painted.
answer: The click is queued as a task. When the stack is empty, the loop runs the listener(s); microtasks drain after each listener returns.
State updates in the handler are usually batched (React batches all updates in one event), so one render follows, not one per setState.
When a frame is due, the browser runs requestAnimationFrame callbacks, then style, layout and paint, then compositing on another thread.
INP measures this whole path: input delay (waiting for earlier tasks) + processing time (your handlers) + presentation delay (render and paint). Good is ≤ 200ms at p75.
Long handlers are the usual cause of bad INP; the fixes are less work, yielding (scheduler.yield()), useTransition for non-urgent updates, or a Worker.

interview.q: A Node service has p99 latency spikes to 2 seconds while average CPU is low. How do you find and fix the cause?
answer: Low average CPU with high tail latency points to short bursts of blocking work, not to lack of capacity. Confirm with event-loop delay (perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay) p99.
Correlate spikes with routes and payload sizes in logs and traces; look for big JSON.parse/JSON.stringify, sync crypto or fs calls, and regexes on user input.
Take a CPU profile under realistic load (node --cpu-prof, Clinic, or the inspector) and read the flame graph for wide sync frames.
Fix by removing the work (smaller payloads, pagination, caching), streaming it, or moving it off the loop (worker_threads, a job queue).
Prevent regressions: body-size limits, an alert on event-loop delay p99, and a load test in CI for the heavy routes.
followups: Why does a slow database query not block the event loop, but a slow regex does?
When would you choose worker_threads over a separate queue service?

interview.q: When would you chunk work with scheduler.yield() and when would you move it to a Web Worker?
answer: Chunking keeps the work on the main thread: easy when it needs the DOM or app state, and the total CPU time is acceptable but must not block input.
A Worker runs on a real second thread: best for long pure computation (parsing, diffing, image or crypto work) that does not need the DOM.
Workers cost message copying (structured clone) unless you transfer ArrayBuffers; for many small messages the overhead can be bigger than the work.
scheduler.yield() keeps the task's priority (continuations run before other queued tasks); setTimeout goes to the back of the line and is clamped to 4ms when nested.
Measure both with the Performance panel and INP from real users; neither helps if the real fix is doing less work.

How would you cancel a long computation running in a Worker?

one: A promise is a placeholder for a future value that settles once: fulfilled or rejected. async/await is syntax on top of it. Most async bugs are about unhandled rejections and accidental sequencing.
an: A restaurant pager. You get it immediately, keep doing other things, and it buzzes once: food ready, or kitchen error.
how: Promise.all (fail fast, all must succeed), allSettled (wait for all, get each outcome), race (first to settle), any (first to succeed).
await inside a for loop runs calls one after another. For independent calls start them all, then await Promise.all(...).
A rejected promise with no handler becomes an unhandled rejection: in Node it crashes the process by default; in browsers it is logged and lost.
Cancellation is not built into promises; use AbortController and pass signal to fetch and your own functions.
why: Request waterfalls, silent failures, race conditions in React effects, and crashed Node servers mostly come from misusing these few tools.
trade: Promise.all with 10,000 items starts 10,000 operations at once. Limit concurrency (p-limit) for real workloads.

plain:
A promise is a box that will contain a result later. It ends in one of two ways: it succeeds with a value, or it fails with an error. async/await is just a nicer way to write code that waits for those boxes.

Most bugs come from two mistakes: waiting for things one by one when they could run together, and forgetting to handle the failure case.
bridge: Every fetch you write returns a promise. React Query and SWR are libraries built mainly to handle promise problems for you: loading state, errors, retries, and old responses arriving late.

walk.title: Loading a dashboard with three API calls
steps: Slow version: const a = await getUser(); const b = await getOrders(); const c = await getStats();. Each call waits for the previous one. 3 × 300ms = 900ms.
Fast version: start all three first, then wait once: const [a, b, c] = await Promise.all([getUser(), getOrders(), getStats()]). Total ≈ 300ms.
But if getStats() fails, Promise.all fails the whole thing, and the user sees nothing.
Better for a dashboard: Promise.allSettled. You get each result separately and can show the user and orders even when stats failed.
If the user leaves the page, cancel the requests with an AbortController so late responses do not update a page that no longer exists.

terms: The three states of a promise: waiting, succeeded, failed.
A promise failed and no code caught the error. In Node this can crash the server.
A built-in object for cancelling fetches and other async work.
A bug where the result depends on which async thing finishes first.
insights: A promise starts its work when it is created, not when you await it. const p = getStats() has already sent the request; await p only waits for the answer. That is why “start all, then await once” is fast.
Promise.all fails fast but does not stop the other calls. They keep running and their results are thrown away. Pass an AbortSignal if they must really stop.
In search boxes, responses can arrive out of order. Always cancel or ignore old requests, or you show results for the wrong query.

prod.summary: In production, promise bugs look like crashed Node processes (unhandled rejections), slow pages (accidental sequential awaits), wrong data on screen (out-of-order responses) and overloaded dependencies (unbounded Promise.all). Seniors check that every promise is awaited or explicitly caught, that independent work runs in parallel with a limit, and that every outgoing call has a timeout.
checklist: Every promise is either awaited, returned, or has its own .catch. ESLint @typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises and no-misused-promises are on.
Every outbound fetch has a timeout, for example signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5000). fetch has no useful timeout by default.
Independent calls run in parallel (Promise.all/allSettled); large fan-outs use a concurrency limit (p-limit, a pool) sized to what the downstream can take.
UI requests are cancelled or ignored when they become stale (route change, new search term) with AbortController.
Errors are wrapped with context: throw new Error('load invoice 42 failed', { cause: err }), so logs show the full chain.
Node has a process.on('unhandledRejection') handler that logs and exits, and the orchestrator restarts the process. Do not just log and continue in an unknown state.
async callbacks are not passed to APIs that ignore the returned promise (array.forEach, event emitters, Express 4 handlers) without catching errors.
numbers: Node.js 15+ default --unhandled-rejections=throw: an unhandled rejection crashes the process.
fetch in browsers and Node has no request timeout you would want by default; you must pass an AbortSignal.
Three independent 300ms calls: ~900ms with sequential awaits, ~300ms with Promise.all.
failures: Node pod restarts with exit code 1 and log Error [ERR_UNHANDLED_REJECTION] or the original error with “triggerUncaughtException”.
A fire-and-forget call like sendAnalytics(event) without await or .catch rejected. Fix: await it, or attach .catch(log) on purpose; turn on no-floating-promises.
A request handler hangs for minutes; connection pool shows all connections busy.
An outbound fetch to a slow partner API had no timeout, so requests piled up. Fix: AbortSignal.timeout(ms) on every call, plus a circuit breaker or fallback.
A nightly job that calls an API for 20,000 users gets HTTP 429 and ECONNRESET errors, then fails.
await Promise.all(users.map(callApi)) started 20,000 requests at once. Fix: limit concurrency (e.g. 10 at a time), add retry with backoff, and use allSettled so one failure does not lose all results.
The checkout page shows the shipping price for the previous address.
Two requests raced; the slower old one resolved last and overwrote state. Fix: abort the previous request on change, or compare a request id before setting state; React Query/SWR do this for you.
Errors inside items.forEach(async (i) => save(i)) are never caught and the function “finishes” before saving.
forEach ignores the returned promises. Fix: for...of with await (sequential) or await Promise.all(items.map(save)) (parallel).

The fetch is cancelled, because race settles as soon as one promise settles

There is no unhandled rejection: race attaches handlers to every input.

interview.q: You need to call a flaky partner API for 10,000 records in a nightly job. How do you write it?
answer: Limit concurrency (a small pool or p-limit, e.g. 5–20) sized to the partner's rate limit, not Promise.all over everything.
Give every call a timeout with AbortSignal.timeout(); fetch has no useful default timeout.
Retry only retryable failures (timeouts, 429, 503) with exponential backoff and jitter, and respect Retry-After; never retry 400s.
Collect per-item outcomes (allSettled style) so one failure does not lose the batch; write failures to a table for a later re-run.
Make each call idempotent (idempotency key or upsert) so retries and re-runs do not create duplicates; log progress so the job can resume.

one: Functions remember the variables from where they were created (closures). this is decided by how a function is called, except arrow functions, which take it from where they were defined.
an: A closure is a backpack a function carries out of the room it was made in, holding the variables it needs. this is a name tag handed to the function by whoever calls it.
how: Lexical scope: inner functions see outer variables. let/const are block-scoped; var is function-scoped and hoisted (as undefined).

A closure captures the variable itself (the binding), not a copy of its value. It keeps that variable alive as long as the function exists. That powers module privacy, factories, memoization and React hooks.

this is set by the call: method call obj.f() → obj; plain call f() → undefined in strict code (ES modules and classes are always strict), the global object in old sloppy scripts; new F() → the new object; f.call(x)/f.bind(x) → x. Arrow functions have no own this; they use the one from where they were written.

Stale closures in React: each render creates new functions that capture that render's props and state. A callback created once (an interval, a socket handler) keeps reading the old values. Fix with a functional updater, a ref, or (React 19.2+) useEffectEvent for logic that must read the latest values without re-running the effect.
why: Stale closures are one of the most common React bugs, and closures explain memory leaks where a callback keeps a huge object alive.
trade: Closures are cheap but retain everything they reference. Long-lived callbacks (listeners, intervals) capturing big data are a classic leak.

myth.m: Arrow functions are just shorter syntax.
myth.r: They also capture this and arguments lexically and cannot be used as constructors.

q.s: A setInterval inside useEffect(() => {...}, []) logs count, but always prints 0 even as count increases. Why?
o: setInterval is broken in React
The callback closed over the count from the first render (stale closure)
count is const
The event loop is blocked
q.e: Use the functional updater, a ref holding the latest value, or include count in dependencies and reset the interval.

more: Prototype chain and classes as sugar
lab: Write a counter factory with a private variable using a closure; prove the variable is not reachable from outside.
Reproduce the classic for (var i...) setTimeout(() => log(i)) bug, then fix it with let.
Reproduce a stale closure in a React interval and fix it two ways.

plain:
When you create a function inside another function, the inner function remembers the variables around it, even after the outer function has finished. That memory is called a closure.

this is different: it is not remembered. It is decided each time, by how the function is called. Arrow functions are the exception: they use the this of the place where they were written.
bridge: Every React hook relies on closures. Each render creates new functions that remember that render's state. A “stale closure” bug is when a callback still remembers an old render's state, for example inside setInterval or an event listener added once.

walk.title: The classic stale-state bug in React
steps: You write useEffect(() => { const id = setInterval(() => console.log(count), 1000); return () => clearInterval(id) }, []).
On the first render, count is 0. The interval callback is created now and remembers count = 0.
The user clicks +1 three times. React renders again with count = 3, but the effect does not run again because its dependency list is empty.
The old callback still runs every second and still prints 0. It reads the count constant of render 1, which is 0 forever: every render has its own count.
Fix: add count to the dependencies (restart the interval), or store the latest value in a useRef, or use setCount(c => c + 1) when you only need to update.

terms: Where a variable can be seen. Inner functions can see outer variables, not the other way round.
A function together with the variables it remembers from where it was created.
Decided by where code is written, not by how it is called.
A special value decided at call time: the object before the dot, or a new object with new.
insights: A closure captures the variable, not a snapshot of its value: if outer code reassigns that variable later, the closure sees the new value. A stale React closure is different: every render has its own count constant, so an old callback keeps the old one.
When a callback “sees old data”, think closure first.
Prefer arrow functions in components and callbacks so this never surprises you; in modern React code you rarely need this at all.

prod.summary: In production, closures cause two kinds of bugs: stale data (a callback keeps using old state or config) and memory leaks (a long-lived callback keeps a large object alive). this bugs mostly appear when a class method is passed as a callback. Seniors review effects, listeners and module-level state with these in mind.
checklist: react-hooks/exhaustive-deps is on and its warnings are fixed, not silenced; if a dependency is left out on purpose there is a comment explaining why.
Callbacks registered once (intervals, WebSocket handlers, global listeners) read changing values through a ref or functional updater, not through a captured variable.
Long-lived closures (listeners, timers, caches) do not capture large objects they do not need, such as a whole response or DOM tree.
Class methods passed as callbacks are arrow-function fields or explicitly bound; otherwise this is undefined when called.
Module-level variables in server code are treated as shared by every request; per-request data never goes there.
No var in new code (ESLint no-var), so loop variables get a fresh binding per iteration.
numbers: let/const in a for loop create a new binding per iteration; var creates one binding for the whole function.
Accessing a let/const before its declaration throws ReferenceError: Cannot access 'x' before initialization (temporal dead zone).
failures: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'items') inside a class method used as button.addEventListener('click', this.handle).
The method was detached from its object, so this is not the instance (it is undefined in classes, which are strict mode). Fix: define handle = () => {...} as a field or pass this.handle.bind(this).
A chat app's WebSocket handler appends new messages to an old list, so earlier messages disappear.
The onmessage handler was set once in an effect with [] deps and closes over the first messages array. Fix: setMessages(prev => [...prev, msg]).
In a Node server, user A sometimes sees user B's data.
A module-level variable (let currentUser) was set per request, but all requests share one module scope and interleave across awaits. Fix: pass context as arguments or use AsyncLocalStorage.
Heap grows with each opened modal; snapshots show old modal data retained by a resize listener closure.
The listener closes over the modal's props and is never removed. Fix: return a cleanup from useEffect that removes the listener; capture only small values.

Wrap the handler in a closure so each request gets its own copy of the module
Move it into a class static field
Use AsyncLocalStorage (or pass the id as a parameter) so each request's async chain carries its own id

undefined and 'A'
'A' and undefined
Both throw TypeError
qs.e: A regular method gets this from the call (obj.), so 'A'. An arrow function takes this from where it was written: the module top level, where this is undefined. The optional chaining avoids the throw. Object literals do not create a this scope.

Zero, because debounce cancels everything on re-render

One per render plus one extra at the end

It logs “undefined”, because the closure captured config before it was assigned
ReferenceError on click, because config is in the temporal dead zone
It logs “dark”

code.title: Editor.tsx

setInterval copies its callback's arguments when it is created
useState resets the form on every render
api.save is called before React commits the state

Adding form to the deps would recreate save and restart the interval on every keystroke. qs.s: An effect opens a WebSocket for roomId and shows a toast in the current theme on each message. Because theme is in the dependency list, changing the theme reconnects the socket. Best fix?
o: Remove theme from the dependency list and disable the lint rule on that line
Keep roomId as the only dependency and read theme through useEffectEvent (React 19.2+) or a ref that always holds the latest value
Wrap the socket in useMemo with [theme]
Store theme in a module-level variable
qs.e: The socket must restart when roomId changes, but not when theme changes. Reading theme through an effect event or a ref gives the latest value without making it a dependency. Removing the dependency and silencing the linter gives a stale theme (the bug comes back silently). A module variable is shared by every component instance.

interview.q: What is a closure? Give me an example of a production bug caused by one.
answer: A function keeps access to the variables of the scope where it was created, even after that scope has returned; it captures the variable, not a snapshot.
Stale closure: an interval or socket handler created once in a React effect keeps reading the first render's state; fix with a functional updater, a ref, or useEffectEvent.
Memory leak: a long-lived listener closes over a big object (a response, a DOM subtree, a chart) and is never removed, so that object can never be collected.
Shared state: a module-level let in a Node server is captured by every request handler, so concurrent requests overwrite each other.
Debugging tip: in a heap snapshot, “(closure)” retainers and the “context” object show exactly which captured variables keep memory alive.

interview.q: How is this decided in JavaScript? When does it bite you in real code?
answer: Rules in order: new → the new object; call/apply/bind → the given value; method call obj.f() → obj; plain call → undefined in strict code.
Arrow functions ignore these rules and use the surrounding this; they cannot be used with new.
Common bug: passing a class method as a callback (addEventListener('click', this.onClick)) loses this; use an arrow-function class field or bind.

Arrow class fields create one function per instance (more memory) and are not on the prototype, so they cannot be overridden with super.method(); methods with bind in the constructor are the alternative.
Modern React function components avoid this completely, which removes this whole class of bugs.

interview.q: In a Node server, how do you make per-request data (request id, user) available deep in the code without passing it through every function?
answer: Never use module-level variables for it: all requests share one module scope and interleave at every await.
Use AsyncLocalStorage from node:async_hooks: als.run(ctx, () => handler()), then als.getStore() anywhere in that async chain.
Logging libraries and OpenTelemetry use the same mechanism to attach trace ids automatically.
Trade-off: it is implicit (hidden dependency), so keep it for cross-cutting data (ids, auth context, tracing), and pass business data as normal arguments.
Watch for code that loses context, such as some connection pools or callback-based libraries; test that the id survives a round trip through your DB client.

one: Two module systems coexist in JavaScript. ES modules (import/export) are the standard and are statically analysable; CommonJS (require) is Node's older dynamic system.
an: ESM is a published table of contents you can read before opening the book. CommonJS is discovering chapters only while reading.
how: ESM imports are static and hoisted, which lets bundlers tree-shake. They load asynchronously and support top-level await. Exports are live bindings.
CommonJS: module.exports, synchronous require, evaluated at runtime, so tree shaking is limited.

Node decides per file: .mjs is ESM and .cjs is CommonJS. For .js it reads the nearest package.json "type" field. With no type, recent Node (22.7+, 20.19+) runs the file as ESM if it contains import/export syntax, but setting type is clearer and faster. exports maps in package.json control entry points for import vs require.

Since Node 20.19 / 22.12, require() can load ES modules without a flag (stable in Node 25.4). It still fails with ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE if the module graph uses top-level await. On older Node you see ERR_REQUIRE_ESM; “Cannot use import statement outside a module” still means a file was treated as CommonJS.
why: Library publishing, build configs, Jest/Vitest setup and Node tooling errors all depend on understanding this split.
trade: Dual-publishing packages (ESM + CJS) avoids breaking consumers but can load two copies of the same library (dual package hazard).

myth.m: TypeScript import syntax means my code runs as ESM.
myth.r: TS can compile import to require. What runs depends on the module setting and the package type. TypeScript 6.0 changed the default module to esnext, so old projects that relied on the CommonJS default can change behaviour when they upgrade.

q.s: Why do bundlers tree-shake ESM much better than CommonJS?
o: ESM is newer
ESM imports/exports are static, so unused exports can be proven unused at build time
CommonJS is slower
ESM files are smaller
q.e: require can be called conditionally with computed names, so the bundler cannot know what is used.

lab: Create a tiny package exporting one function, publish-ready for both ESM and CJS using exports conditions. Import it from an ESM and a CJS consumer.
Read the exports field of a popular package in node_modules and explain each condition.

plain:
A module is one file that shares some things (exports) and uses things from other files (imports). JavaScript has two systems. The modern one is ES modules: import and export. The old Node one is CommonJS: require and module.exports.

They mostly work together, but when they do not, you get confusing errors. Knowing which one a file uses solves most of them.
bridge: Vite and Next.js projects are ES modules. Some older npm packages and config files (.cjs, old Jest setups) are CommonJS. Errors like “Cannot use import statement outside a module”, or on older Node “require() of ES Module not supported”, are this mismatch.

walk.title: Why one import made your bundle 70KB bigger
steps: You write import _ from 'lodash' and use one function, _.debounce.
lodash is published as CommonJS. The bundler cannot know for sure which parts you use, so it includes the whole library.
You switch to import debounce from 'lodash-es/debounce' (an ES module build).
Now the bundler can see exactly which export is used and drops the rest (tree shaking).
Your bundle analyzer shows the library shrink from about 70KB to about 2KB.

terms: ES modules: import/export. The official standard, used in browsers and modern Node.
The bundler removing exports you never import.
A field that tells Node and bundlers which file to load for import vs require.
insights: Static imports are what make tree shaking possible. Dynamic require with variables cannot be analysed.
Use dynamic import() on purpose to split heavy code into a separate chunk loaded later.
When a library behaves differently in tests and in the app, check whether the test runner loads its CJS build and the bundler loads its ESM build.

prod.summary: In production, module problems appear at the edges: a library that works in the app but breaks in tests, a server that crashes at startup with a module error after a dependency upgrade, a bundle that is 200KB larger than needed, or two copies of React. Seniors keep the project on one module system (ESM for new code), read exports maps of dependencies, and check bundle analysis on every major dependency change.
checklist: The project has one clear module type: "type": "module" in package.json for new Node code, and TypeScript module/moduleResolution set explicitly (nodenext for Node, bundler for Vite/Next).
Published libraries define an exports map with types, import and require conditions, and are checked with a tool like “Are the Types Wrong?” (attw).
Libraries set "sideEffects": false (or list real side-effect files) so bundlers can drop unused modules.
Bundle analysis (e.g. rollup-plugin-visualizer, @next/bundle-analyzer) runs when dependencies change; a big CJS-only dependency is a red flag.
npm ls react (or the same for any stateful library) shows a single copy; duplicates cause “Invalid hook call” and broken singletons.
Heavy, rarely used code (charts, editors, PDF) is loaded with dynamic import() so it becomes a separate chunk.
Node runtime version supports the module features you use: require(esm) needs Node 20.19+ or 22.12+.
numbers: Node.js: require(esm) unflagged in v20.19.0 / v22.12.0 / v23.0.0, stable since v25.4.0.
Node.js runs .ts files directly with type stripping by default since v22.18.0 / v23.6.0 (stable in v24.12 / v25.2); it ignores tsconfig.json and rejects enum and parameter properties.
TypeScript 6.0 (March 2026) defaults: module: esnext, moduleResolution node10 deprecated in favour of nodenext or bundler.
failures: Server crashes at startup: Error [ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE]: require() cannot be used on an ESM graph with top-level await.
A CommonJS file require()s a dependency whose new ESM version uses top-level await. Fix: load it with await import(), or migrate the caller to ESM.
Works in the app, fails in Jest with SyntaxError: Cannot use import statement outside a module from a file in node_modules.
Jest runs CommonJS and does not transform node_modules by default; the dependency ships only ESM. Fix: switch to Vitest (native ESM), or add the package to transformIgnorePatterns exceptions.
“Invalid hook call” errors in a monorepo, or instanceof checks failing for a class from a shared library.

Two copies of the library were loaded (ESM and CJS builds, or two versions): the dual package hazard. Fix: dedupe (npm ls, resolutions/overrides, bundler resolve.dedupe), keep stateful packages as peer dependencies.
Bundle grows by 70KB after adding one helper function import.

The dependency is CommonJS or marks itself as having side effects, so the bundler keeps everything. Fix: use its ESM build or per-function import path, or pick a smaller library; check with the bundle analyzer.
ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND in Node for import './utils' that works in Vite.

The package's exports map is broken

Mark the library as a devDependency

o: Node cannot run code compiled by tsc
The bundler setting makes tsc emit CommonJS

interview.q: What are the differences between ES modules and CommonJS that matter in production?
answer: ESM is static: imports are known before the code runs, which enables tree shaking and early errors. CJS require is a runtime function call, so it can be conditional and computed.
ESM exports are live bindings; CJS gives you whatever value module.exports had when you read it.
ESM loading is asynchronous and supports top-level await; CJS is synchronous. That is why require() of an ESM graph with top-level await fails with ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE.
ESM in Node needs full relative paths with extensions and has no __dirname (use import.meta.dirname, Node 20.11+).
Mixing both can load two copies of a package (dual package hazard): broken singletons, failing instanceof, “Invalid hook call”.
followups: How do circular imports behave differently in ESM and CJS?
Why can a bundler not tree-shake most CJS code?

interview.q: You are publishing a new internal library in 2026. ESM-only or dual ESM + CJS?
answer: Default to ESM-only if all consumers run Node 20.19+/22.12+ or a bundler: require(esm) lets CJS consumers load it, as long as the library has no top-level await.
Dual publishing doubles the build and test matrix and brings the dual package hazard; choose it only for consumers stuck on older runtimes or tools.
Either way, define exports with types first in each condition, set sideEffects, and set engines.node.
Check the published package with attw (Are the Types Wrong?) and publint in CI, and test install from a packed tarball, not from the source folder.
Adding or tightening exports is a breaking change (deep imports stop working): release it as a major version.
followups: What exactly is the dual package hazard and how do you avoid it?
How would Jest users consume an ESM-only package?

interview.q: How does tree shaking work, and what silently breaks it?
answer: The bundler builds a graph of static imports/exports, marks exports that nobody imports as unused, and the minifier drops them if removing them cannot change behaviour.
It breaks with CommonJS dependencies, namespace or default imports of huge objects (import _ from 'lodash'), and barrel files that re-export everything with side effects.
Top-level side effects (polyfills, registering globals, CSS imports) force a module to stay unless the package declares "sideEffects" correctly.
Verify with a bundle analyzer and a size budget in CI, instead of trusting that it works.
Code splitting with dynamic import() is the other half: tree shaking removes unused code, splitting delays code that is used rarely.
followups: Why can a wrong sideEffects: false break an app?
Are barrel files always bad?

one: JS frees memory automatically once nothing can reach an object. Leaks happen when something long-lived keeps a reference you forgot about.
an: A cleaner throws away anything nobody is holding a string to. A leak is a forgotten string tied from the front door to a pile of junk.
how: V8's collector is generational. New objects go to the small young generation, which a fast copying “scavenger” cleans often. Objects that survive are moved to the old generation, which is cleaned less often with mark-sweep-compact, mostly in parallel and concurrently with your code.

Common leaks: event listeners never removed, intervals never cleared, growing caches/maps without eviction, detached DOM nodes held in variables, closures capturing large objects, subscriptions not unsubscribed in React effects.
In Node a leak shows as steadily rising heap until FATAL ERROR: Reached heap limit Allocation failed - JavaScript heap out of memory or a container OOMKill.
WeakMap/WeakRef hold references that do not prevent collection.
why: Long-running SPAs (dashboards left open all day) and Node servers both suffer. Seniors are expected to find leaks with heap snapshots, not guess.
trade: GC pauses are usually small, but huge heaps and churny allocation in hot paths can cause latency spikes.

myth.r: They cannot leak unreachable memory. They leak reachable memory you no longer need, which is the common kind.

q.s: A Node API's memory grows 50MB per hour and never drops. Code has const cache = new Map() at module level storing results by request URL. Diagnosis?
o: GC is broken
An unbounded cache: every unique URL adds an entry that is never evicted
Too many CPU cores
HTTP/2
q.e: Use an LRU with a max size or TTL, or an external cache like Redis.

lab: In a React app, add a window resize listener in an effect without cleanup, mount/unmount the component 50 times, and find the leak in a DevTools heap snapshot comparison. Then fix it.
In Node, create an unbounded Map cache, load test it, take two heap snapshots (--inspect) and find the Map in the comparison.

plain:
JavaScript cleans up memory for you. The garbage collector looks for objects that no code can reach anymore and frees them.

A memory leak happens when you no longer need something, but some code can still reach it: a listener you never removed, a timer you never cleared, a cache that keeps growing. The collector cannot free it, so memory grows until the tab or server becomes slow or crashes.
bridge: In React the most common leak is an effect without cleanup: window.addEventListener or setInterval in useEffect without returning a function that removes it. Every time the component mounts again, one more listener stays alive.

walk.title: Finding a leak in a dashboard left open all day
steps: Users say the admin dashboard gets slow after a few hours. You open DevTools → Memory.
Take a heap snapshot. Use the app for a minute (open and close a chart panel 20 times). Take a second snapshot.
Compare the two. You see 20 copies of a chart object and 20 resize listeners that should not exist.
The “Retainers” view shows the path keeping them alive: window → resize listener → closure → chart.
You add return () => window.removeEventListener('resize', onResize) to the effect. A new snapshot shows the count stays at 1.

terms: The engine part that frees memory no code can reach.
Can be found by following references from global variables, the stack, or live listeners.
A picture of every object in memory at one moment, viewable in DevTools.
The object holding a reference that keeps another object alive.
insights: Memory that only goes up and never comes down after GC is the signal of a leak. Normal memory goes up and down like a saw.
Any cache without a size limit or expiry is a leak waiting for enough traffic.

WeakMap is the right tool for attaching extra data to objects you do not own (DOM nodes, request objects): when the key object is collected, its entry goes too. It is not a cache you can size or list.

prod.summary: In production, memory problems show up as a Node pod that is OOMKilled every few days, or a dashboard tab that becomes slow after hours. The signal is memory that rises after every GC and never returns to its baseline. Seniors compare heap snapshots instead of guessing, bound every cache, and set the Node heap limit to fit the container.
checklist: Every in-process cache has a max size and/or TTL (e.g. lru-cache with max), or the data lives in Redis.
Every addEventListener, setInterval, subscription and observer in an effect has a matching cleanup.
Node heap limit fits the container: --max-old-space-size (in MiB) leaves room for buffers, native memory and the stack, so V8 fails with a heap error you can see instead of a silent kernel OOMKill.
Dashboards graph heap used after GC (process.memoryUsage().heapUsed, or nodejs_heap_size_used_bytes from prom-client) and RSS per pod; alert on a steady upward trend, not on one spike.
Production can produce a heap snapshot on demand or near the limit (--heapsnapshot-near-heap-limit=1) and someone knows how to read retainers in DevTools.
Large responses are streamed instead of buffered whole into memory (res.arrayBuffer() of a 500MB file will crash a 512Mi pod).
SPA soak test: open and close the heaviest view 50 times, force GC, and check the heap returns near its start.
numbers: Kubernetes reports an OOM-killed container as OOMKilled with exit code 137 (128 + SIGKILL 9).
Node's --max-old-space-size is in MiB, e.g. --max-old-space-size=384 for a 512Mi container.
Node: --heapsnapshot-near-heap-limit writes heap snapshots just before running out of memory (no longer experimental in v22.22.1 / v24.13.1 / v25.4.0).
failures: Pods restart every ~3 days with OOMKilled, exit code 137; memory graph is a slow straight line upward.
A module-level Map caches by URL, including query strings, so it never stops growing. Fix: bounded LRU with TTL, key on normalised input, or move the cache to Redis.
FATAL ERROR: Reached heap limit Allocation failed - JavaScript heap out of memory in a CI build or a batch job.
The job loads a whole dataset into one array, or the default heap limit is below what the job truly needs. Fix first: stream or batch the data. Only then raise --max-old-space-size.
A dashboard tab reaches 2GB after a day; the heap snapshot shows thousands of “Detached HTMLDivElement”.

A chart library instance is stored in a module variable or listener after its component unmounted, so the removed DOM cannot be collected. Fix: call the library's destroy() in effect cleanup and drop the reference.
p99 latency spikes every few seconds in a Node service that allocates many short objects per request.

GC work from high allocation rate (e.g. building large intermediate arrays, JSON stringify of huge objects). Fix: profile with --trace-gc or the DevTools allocation timeline, reduce allocations in the hot path, stream large payloads.

code.title: A bounded cache instead of a leaking Map
code.note: max is what stops the leak; TTL alone does not, because entries are only removed when they expire and new keys can arrive faster. .unref() lets the process exit even though the interval exists.

qs.s: A Node container has a 512Mi memory limit. It is killed with OOMKilled (137), but logs never show a “heap out of memory” error. What is the most likely reason?
o: V8's heap limit is higher than the container allows, so the kernel kills the process before V8 reaches its own limit
V8 has no heap limit in containers
The process has a CPU leak, not a memory leak
Exit code 137 means an unhandled promise rejection
qs.e: RSS includes heap, buffers and native memory. If the V8 heap limit plus everything else is above 512Mi, the kernel's OOM killer acts first, with no JS error. Set --max-old-space-size below the limit to get a visible heap error and a snapshot.

qs.s: Memory graph of a Node service: after each GC it drops back to ~180MB, but between GCs it climbs to 400MB. This repeats all day. What does it show?
o: A memory leak that will crash soon
Normal behaviour: lots of short-lived garbage that GC collects. Watch the post-GC baseline, which is flat
The GC is broken and must be tuned
The heap limit is too small
qs.e: A saw-tooth with a flat bottom is healthy. A leak is a rising bottom: each GC leaves more behind. If the high allocation rate causes latency, reduce allocation, but it is not a leak.

qs.s: You store extra metadata for DOM nodes in const meta = new Map<Element, Info>(). Nodes are removed from the page, but memory keeps growing. Smallest correct fix?
o: Call meta.clear() every minute
Use a WeakRef for each Info value
Use a WeakMap<Element, Info>, so the entry can be collected when the element is no longer reachable elsewhere
Use an object instead of a Map
qs.e: A Map key is a strong reference, so it keeps removed elements alive. A WeakMap key does not. Clearing every minute loses live data. WeakRef on values does not help, because the strong key is the problem.

qs.s: This Server-Sent Events endpoint leaks memory: heap grows with every client that connects and disconnects. Which fix is correct?

code.title: events.ts

o: Call global.gc() after each request
Make subscribe return an unsubscribe function and call it on req.on('close'), so the closure and its res can be collected
Store listeners in a WeakSet so they disappear automatically
Set --max-old-space-size higher
qs.e: The module-level Set holds each closure, and each closure holds its res (socket, buffers). Nothing ever removes them, so they stay reachable. GC cannot free reachable objects, so global.gc() does nothing. A WeakSet would let the listener be collected while the client is still connected (nothing else holds it), and it cannot be iterated to broadcast anyway.

qs.s: You compare two DevTools heap snapshots taken before and after opening and closing a report view 20 times. Where should you look first?

code.title: Comparison view (snapshot 2 vs snapshot 1)
code.src:
Constructor        # New   # Deleted   # Delta   Size Delta
(closure)          2,000       1,980       +20       +1.6 KB
Array              3,100       3,050       +50       +2.1 KB
Detached <div>     1,000           0    +1,000       +0.5 MB
ChartInstance         20           0       +20      +38.0 MB

o: Array, because it has the most new objects
(closure), because closures are the usual cause of leaks
Detached <div>, because DOM nodes are always the root cause
ChartInstance: 20 created, none deleted, 38MB. Open its Retainers to see what still holds it (a listener, a module variable, a store)
qs.e: Look for objects that are created on every cycle and never deleted, and that carry the most memory. One ChartInstance per open, none freed, is the leak; the detached divs are probably kept alive by the charts. Arrays and closures are mostly created and deleted in equal numbers, which is normal churn.

qs.s: A Node service runs in a container with a 1Gi memory limit and handles large file uploads in Buffers. Which heap setting is most reasonable?
o: --max-old-space-size=1024, to use the whole limit
--max-old-space-size=4096, so V8 never throws heap errors
Around --max-old-space-size=640–768, leaving room for Buffers, native memory and code outside the V8 heap
--max-old-space-size=64, so GC runs often and memory stays low
qs.e: RSS = V8 heap + memory outside it (Buffer/ArrayBuffer data, native addons, thread stacks, code). If the heap may grow to the full 1Gi, the kernel OOM-kills the pod (exit 137) with no JS error. Node's docs suggest leaving headroom (e.g. 1536MB on a 2GiB machine); with large Buffers leave more. 64MB would cause constant GC and heap-out-of-memory crashes.

qs.s: A developer wants to use FinalizationRegistry to close database connections when the wrapper object is garbage-collected. What do you say in review?
o: Good idea: finalizers run right after an object becomes unreachable
Fine, but only in Node, not in browsers
Fine if you also call global.gc() regularly

No: GC may run late or never for a given object, so cleanup is not guaranteed. Close explicitly in try/finally (or with a using declaration where supported); use finalizers only as a backup to log leaks
qs.e: The spec makes no promise about when, or whether, finalization callbacks run. A pool can run out of connections long before GC happens. Scarce resources (connections, file handles, locks) need deterministic cleanup. global.gc() needs a flag and still does not guarantee callback timing.

interview.q: A Node service is OOMKilled every few days. Walk me through your investigation.
answer: Confirm the pattern: graph heap used and RSS per pod over days. A rising post-GC baseline is a leak; a flat baseline with spikes is load or one big request.
Check whether heap or non-heap grows: heap growth points to JS objects; RSS growth with a flat heap points to Buffers, native addons or many sockets.
Set --max-old-space-size below the container limit so V8 fails visibly, and enable --heapsnapshot-near-heap-limit or take snapshots on demand.
Compare two snapshots taken some time apart under load; sort by size delta and follow the Retainers path to a module-level Map, listener, or cache.
Fix the root cause (bounded LRU, cleanup on close, streaming), then verify with a soak test, and alert on the post-GC trend instead of waiting for OOM.
followups: How do you take a heap snapshot safely in production? It pauses the process.
What does exit code 137 tell you, and what does it not?

interview.q: How does V8's garbage collector work, and why should an application developer care?
answer: It is generational: most objects die young, so new objects go to a small young space cleaned often by a fast copying scavenger.
Survivors are promoted to the old space, collected by mark-sweep-compact, mostly concurrently and in parallel on helper threads, with short main-thread pauses.
Reachability is the only rule: anything reachable from roots (globals, stack, live closures, listeners, timers) stays.
High allocation rates in hot paths mean more frequent GC and latency jitter; huge heaps mean longer marking work.
Practical result: avoid unbounded structures, avoid giant intermediate arrays and strings per request, stream large data, and measure with --trace-gc or the allocation profiler.
followups: What is a “detached DOM node” and how does it stay alive?
When are WeakMap and WeakRef the right tool?

interview.q: How do you find and prevent memory leaks in a single-page app that stays open all day?
answer: Reproduce with a repeatable action loop (open/close a view 20–50 times), force GC, and compare heap snapshots before and after.
Typical retainers: listeners on window/document, intervals, WebSocket or store subscriptions, third-party widgets without destroy(), global caches.
Every effect that subscribes returns a cleanup; libraries with imperative instances are destroyed on unmount.
Use WeakMap for metadata attached to DOM nodes or objects you do not own.
Add a soak test (Playwright plus performance.memory or CDP heap metrics) to catch regressions before users do.
followups: Why might a leak not show up in React Strict Mode tests?
How would you report memory from real users?

t: How JS engines run your code
one: Engines like V8 parse your code, start running it in an interpreter, then compile hot functions into optimised machine code based on the types they observe.
an: A translator who first reads a speech aloud line by line, then, noticing some paragraphs repeat constantly, writes a polished pre-translated version of just those, and throws it away if the speaker changes the wording.
how: Parse → bytecode (Ignition interpreter) → hot functions get optimised by JIT compilers (Sparkplug, Maglev, TurboFan in V8).
Optimisation relies on hidden classes (object shapes) and inline caches. Objects created with the same properties in the same order share a shape and fast property access.
If assumptions break (a function suddenly receives a different type), the engine deoptimises back to slower code.
Parsing and compiling large bundles costs real CPU time on phones before any of your code runs.
why: Explains why JS bundle size hurts more than image size, and why consistent object shapes and monomorphic hot functions matter in performance-critical code.
trade: Micro-optimising for the JIT is rarely worth it in app code; it matters in libraries, game loops, parsers and data-heavy hot paths. Measure first.

myth.m: JavaScript is interpreted, so it is always slow.
myth.r: Hot paths are JIT-compiled to machine code. Most slowness comes from doing too much work or too much JS, not from the language.

q.s: Why is 300KB of JavaScript more expensive for a phone than a 300KB image?
o: It is not
JS must be parsed and compiled, then executed on the main thread, where it blocks input; an image is mostly decoded off the main thread and just displayed
Images are cached
JS cannot be compressed
q.e: Byte for byte, JS costs CPU time, and its execution blocks interactivity. Modern engines move some parsing and compiling off the main thread, but running the code always happens on it.

more: WebAssembly as an alternative for hot code
lab: Record a Performance trace of a page load and find the "Compile Script" and "Evaluate Script" time.
Run node --trace-deopt on a function you call with mixed types and see deopt messages.

V8 blog: The cost of JavaScript in 2019
V8 blog: Maglev, V8's fastest optimizing JIT

plain:
Your JS file is just text. The browser engine (V8 in Chrome and Node) has to read it, turn it into instructions, and run it. It starts running slowly but quickly, then watches which functions run often and compiles those into fast machine code.

This is why large JavaScript bundles hurt: before your app does anything, the phone must download, read and prepare all that code.
bridge: In the DevTools Performance panel you have probably seen yellow blocks called “Evaluate Script” and “Compile Script” at page load. That is the engine preparing your bundle. On a cheap Android phone it can take seconds.

walk.title: From bundle to running code on a phone
steps: The browser downloads app.js (say 400KB compressed, 1.5MB uncompressed).
The engine parses the text into a structure it understands. On a slow phone this alone can take hundreds of milliseconds.
It compiles to bytecode and starts running it in the interpreter. Your app begins to work.
Functions called many times (for example, a list item renderer) are noticed as “hot” and compiled into optimised machine code.
If a hot function suddenly receives a different kind of data, the engine throws the optimised version away (deoptimises) and slows down again.

terms: Google's JavaScript engine, used in Chrome, Node and Deno.
Just-in-time compiler: turns hot code into machine code while the program runs.
A compact instruction format the interpreter runs before full optimisation.
Falling back to slower code when the engine's assumptions break.
insights: 100KB of JavaScript costs far more than 100KB of image, because JS must also be parsed, compiled and executed.
Most app slowness is too much work or too much code, not the engine. Ship less JS before micro-optimising.
One deoptimisation is normal and cheap. It hurts when the same hot function is optimised and deoptimised again and again; --trace-deopt shows that pattern.

prod.summary: In production, engine internals matter in two places. On the frontend, the cost of parsing, compiling and running your bundle on cheap phones decides how fast the page becomes usable. On the backend and in libraries, hot functions that keep stable object shapes stay fast, while ones that see many shapes or trigger deoptimisation burn CPU. Seniors measure with profilers first and only then shape code for the JIT.
checklist: There is a JS budget per route (for example, compressed JS size per page) enforced in CI with a tool like size-limit or bundler output checks.
Performance traces are recorded with 4x–6x CPU throttling to approximate a mid-range Android phone; check “Evaluate Script” and “Compile Code” time.
Hot paths (parsers, render loops, data transforms over 100k items) create objects with the same properties in the same order, ideally from one constructor or factory.
Hot functions are not fed many different object shapes; no delete obj.prop on hot objects (set to undefined instead).
Node CPU problems are profiled (node --cpu-prof, 0x, Clinic.js flame graphs) before anyone rewrites code “for speed”.
Static assets are served with long-lived caching so V8's code cache can reuse compiled code on repeat visits.
numbers: V8 tiers: Ignition (interpreter) → Sparkplug (baseline compiler) → Maglev (mid-tier optimising, shipped in Chrome 117) → TurboFan (top tier).
Inline caches: monomorphic = 1 shape seen, polymorphic = 2–4 shapes, megamorphic = more than 4, which falls back to a slower generic lookup.
A long task is > 50ms; a big bundle's “Evaluate Script” on a low-end phone easily exceeds that in one block.
failures: Lighthouse on mobile shows high Total Blocking Time; the trace shows one 1.2s “Evaluate Script” block at load.

The whole app, including admin pages and a charting library, is in one entry bundle. Fix: route-level code splitting, dynamic import() for heavy widgets, remove unused dependencies, and check the result with a bundle analyzer.
A hot JSON-transform function got 5x slower after a refactor; --trace-deopt prints repeated deopts for it.

The new code builds objects with properties added in different orders or conditionally, so the function sees many shapes and goes megamorphic. Fix: create objects with all fields in one literal, same order, using undefined for missing values.
Node service CPU rises sharply after adding a per-request delete res.internalField on large response objects used in a hot loop.

Deleting a property that is not the last one added usually switches the object to slow “dictionary mode”, so later property access in hot code is slower. Fix: build a new object without the field (const { internalField, ...rest } = obj) or set it to undefined, then confirm with a CPU profile.
A page is fast on developer MacBooks but users on budget phones report 5–8s before buttons work.
Developers test on CPUs several times faster than users' devices; parse/compile/execute time scales with CPU. Fix: test with CPU throttling, use real-user metrics (INP, long tasks), and ship less JS.

code.title: Stable shapes in a hot path
code.note: This matters only in code that runs millions of times. Measure with a CPU profile before changing normal app code.

qs.s: A team cuts their bundle from 900KB to 450KB of compressed JS by removing a library. Users on budget Android phones report the page becomes interactive much sooner, even on fast Wi-Fi. Why?
o: Less JS means less parsing, compiling and executing on a slow CPU, which was the bottleneck, not the network
Wi-Fi speed does not matter for JS at all
Smaller bundles are cached by the CDN, larger ones are not
The browser skips the JIT for small bundles
qs.e: On fast networks, the CPU cost of JS dominates on weak devices. Download time halved too, but with fast Wi-Fi that was already small; the main-thread time is what users felt.

qs.s: In a hot function, function area(s) { return s.w * s.h } is called with 8 different object shapes (from different factories). What does V8 most likely do?
o: Compile 8 separate optimised copies of the function
Throw an error after 4 shapes
The property access becomes megamorphic and uses a slower generic lookup
Convert all objects to the same hidden class automatically
qs.e: Inline caches handle one shape (monomorphic) or a few (polymorphic, up to 4) quickly. Beyond that, the site becomes megamorphic. Making all inputs share one shape fixes it.

qs.s: Your Node API profile shows 30% of CPU in JSON.parse and a regex inside one handler. A colleague suggests rewriting loops to “help the JIT”. What should you do first?
o: Rewrite the loops; the JIT benefits every loop
Switch to WebAssembly for the whole service
Add more pods; CPU optimisation is never worth it
Attack the measured hot spots: avoid re-parsing, reduce payload size, and fix or precompile the regex
qs.e: Profile-driven work beats guessing. The JIT already optimises simple loops well; the time is in specific operations you can avoid or shrink. More pods treat the symptom and cost money.

qs.s: len is hot and has only ever seen Vec objects. Then a rarely used path calls it once with an object literal. What does V8 most likely do?

code.title: vec.js

o: The optimised code may deoptimise once; the property access becomes polymorphic (2 shapes), which is still fast
len becomes megamorphic forever and runs at interpreter speed
V8 reorders the literal's properties to match Vec
V8 throws a TypeError because the shapes differ
qs.e: { y, x } has a different hidden class than a Vec (different order and origin). The optimised code assumed one shape, so it can bail out and later reoptimise with two. Two shapes is polymorphic, which inline caches handle well; megamorphic starts after 4. One rare extra shape is not worth refactoring for.

qs.s: You run node --trace-deopt bench.js and see this line repeated many times. What does it tell you?

code.title: node --trace-deopt (shortened)
code.src:
[bailout (kind: deopt-eager, reason: wrong map): begin. deoptimizing
  <JSFunction total (sfi = 0x2c1f...)>, opt id 3, bytecode offset 14, ...]
[bailout (kind: deopt-eager, reason: wrong map): begin. deoptimizing
  <JSFunction total (sfi = 0x2c1f...)>, opt id 5, bytecode offset 14, ...]

o: The function ran out of memory
A source map is missing, so V8 cannot map the code
Optimised total received an object whose hidden class (V8 calls it a “map”) it did not expect, so V8 threw away the optimised code; it keeps happening, so inputs have unstable shapes
A garbage collection interrupted the function
qs.e: In V8, a “map” is the hidden class (object shape). “wrong map” means a shape check in optimised code failed. Repeated deopts of the same function mean it keeps getting new shapes: look at where its inputs are created and make them use one literal or class with the same fields in the same order.

qs.s: Your SPA deploys every hour and the single main.[hash].js (1.2MB) changes each time, even when only app code changed. Returning users on phones see long “Compile Script” time after every deploy. What helps most?
o: Turn off minification so the browser parses faster
Split stable vendor code into its own content-hashed chunk, so it keeps the same URL and the browser can reuse its cached file and V8's compiled code cache
Serve the bundle with Cache-Control: no-store so it is always fresh
Inline the whole bundle in the HTML
qs.e: Chrome caches compiled code for scripts it has seen before, tied to the script resource. If every deploy changes all of the bytes, that cache is useless. Separating rarely-changing vendor code keeps most bytes, and their compiled code, reusable. no-store and inlining remove caching completely.

qs.s: Which statement about these two arrays in V8 is true?

code.title: arrays.js

o: Both end up identical once filled
b is slower because push reallocates every time
a is stored as a hash table because it is large
a starts “holey” and stays holey even after it is filled; b stays packed small integers, so reads from b need fewer checks
qs.e: V8 tracks an “elements kind” per array. new Array(n) creates holes, and an array never goes back from holey to packed. Reads from holey arrays must check for holes and the prototype chain. push grows capacity in steps, not on every call. The difference matters only in very hot code; measure before changing app code.

interview.q: Why is 1MB of JavaScript more expensive than a 1MB image, and how would you reduce the cost?
answer: Both must download, but JS must also be parsed, compiled and executed, and execution happens on the main thread, which blocks input.
Images are decoded mostly off the main thread and do not block interactivity in the same way.
On low-end Android phones CPU time per KB is several times higher than on a developer laptop, so test with CPU throttling and real-user data (INP, long tasks).
Reduce: route-level code splitting, dynamic import() for heavy widgets, removing dependencies, server rendering with less client JS (React Server Components), and a JS size budget in CI.
Keep caching effective: content-hashed, stable vendor chunks so the browser can reuse files and compiled code across visits.

interview.q: What are hidden classes and inline caches? When should an application developer care?
answer: V8 gives objects with the same properties added in the same order the same hidden class (“map”), so property offsets are known.
Inline caches remember the shapes seen at each property access: 1 shape is monomorphic (fastest), 2–4 polymorphic, more is megamorphic (generic, slower lookup).
Optimising compilers (Maglev, TurboFan) specialise code on those shapes; a new shape can trigger a deopt.
Care only in measured hot paths: parsers, data transforms over large arrays, render loops, library internals. Use one class or literal shape, avoid delete, and do not mix types in one field.
For normal app code, doing less work and shipping less JS matters far more.
followups: What does a deopt cost?
How would you check whether a function is optimised?

interview.q: A hot Node function became 5x slower after a refactor. How do you investigate?
answer: Reproduce with a benchmark on realistic data, and compare the before and after commits with the same Node version.
Take CPU profiles (node --cpu-prof, flame graphs) to see where time moved; it is often not where the diff is.
Check for deopts with --trace-deopt (and --trace-opt) and for new shapes, delete, arguments tricks, or try/catch in odd places that older advice warned about.
Check allocation: new intermediate arrays, spreads in loops, or string building can make GC the real cost (--trace-gc).
Fix the cause, add the benchmark to CI or a perf test so the regression cannot return silently.
followups: Why can microbenchmarks lie?
When would you consider WebAssembly or a native addon?

one: TypeScript adds static types that are checked at build time and erased at runtime. Its types are structural: shape matters, not names.
an: A building inspector who checks the blueprints. Once the house is built, the inspector leaves; nothing guards the doors at runtime.
how: Structural typing: any object with the right properties fits an interface, whatever its declared name.
Unions ('idle' | 'loading' | 'error') and narrowing with typeof, in, equality checks, and custom type guards.
Discriminated unions: {status:'ok', data} | {status:'err', error} make impossible states unrepresentable, and exhaustive switches with never catch missing cases.
unknown (must narrow before use) vs any (turns checking off). strict mode should be on; since TypeScript 6.0 it is the default, but older projects often set it to false explicitly.
why: Good types encode business rules and catch whole classes of bugs before runtime. Leads set the conventions everyone else follows.
trade: Types vanish at runtime, so data from the network, forms and env vars must be validated at the boundary. Over-clever types slow the team down.

myth.m: If it compiles in TypeScript, the data is that type at runtime.
myth.r: Only if every boundary was validated. const user = (await res.json()) as User is a promise to the compiler, not a check.

q.s: Which type best prevents a component from having both data and error set, or loading with data?
o: { loading: boolean; data?: T; error?: Error }
A discriminated union: { status: 'loading' } | { status: 'success'; data: T } | { status: 'error'; error: Error }
any
Record<string, unknown>
q.e: Each state carries exactly its own fields, so impossible combinations do not type-check.

more: Type inference and when to annotate
lab: Model a payment flow's states as a discriminated union and write an exhaustive switch with a never check. Add a new state and watch the compiler point at every place to update.
Turn on strict and noUncheckedIndexedAccess in a project and fix the new errors.

plain:
TypeScript checks your code before it runs. It reads your types and says “this value might be undefined here” or “this function expects a number”. When the code runs in the browser, all types are gone. It is just JavaScript.

TypeScript cares about the shape of data, not its name. If an object has the right properties, it fits.
bridge: You already use types for props: type ButtonProps = { label: string; onClick: () => void }. The next level is using types to make wrong states impossible, for example a request that is “loading” and also has “data” at the same time.

walk.title: Making impossible states impossible
steps: Weak type: { loading: boolean; data?: User; error?: string }. This allows nonsense like loading: true with both data and error.
Better type: { status: 'loading' } | { status: 'success'; data: User } | { status: 'error'; error: string }.
Now in your component, if (state.status === 'success') TypeScript knows state.data exists. In the other branches, it does not let you touch it.
Add a switch (state.status) with a final default: { const _exhaustive: never = state; return _exhaustive; }.
Later someone adds { status: 'empty' }. The compiler immediately shows every place that forgot to handle it.

terms: Types match by shape (properties), not by name.
A value that can be one of several types: A | B.
TypeScript learning a more exact type after a check like if (x.status === 'ok').
A type with no values; useful to prove every case was handled.
insights: Structural typing means a Customer and an Employee with the same fields are interchangeable to the compiler. Where mixing them is dangerous (IDs, money), use branded types.
any switches checking off and spreads. Prefer unknown and narrow it.
A good type removes the need for a runtime check and a test. A bad type gives false confidence.

prod.summary: In a production codebase, the type system is a team tool. The important decisions are the compiler settings, how much any and as are allowed, and whether types describe real states of the business. Seniors keep strict on, make CI fail on type errors, and push validation to the boundaries so internal types can be trusted.
checklist: tsconfig has strict: true (default since TS 6.0) and, for new code, noUncheckedIndexedAccess and exactOptionalPropertyTypes considered.
CI runs tsc --noEmit (or the framework's typecheck) and fails the build on errors; bundlers like Vite and esbuild strip types without checking them.
any is banned by lint (@typescript-eslint/no-explicit-any, no-unsafe-* rules); unknown plus narrowing is used for outside data.
as casts and ! non-null assertions are rare and each one is justified in review.
State with several phases (requests, payments, wizards) is modelled as a discriminated union with an exhaustive never check.
Data from outside (API, forms, env, storage) gets a runtime schema; the TS type is inferred from it, not written separately.
numbers: TypeScript 6.0 (March 2026) made strict: true, module: esnext and types: [] the defaults.
TypeScript 7.0 (July 2026) is the native Go port of the compiler; Microsoft reports full builds typically about 10x faster.
Turning on noUncheckedIndexedAccess makes arr[i] and record[key] return T | undefined.
failures: Production error TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'name') in code that “type-checks fine”.
const user = users[0] is typed User, but the array was empty. Fix: enable noUncheckedIndexedAccess and handle the undefined case.
Build passes in CI and deploys, but the editor shows red errors everywhere.
CI only runs vite build/esbuild, which strip types without checking. Fix: add tsc --noEmit as a required CI step.
A new order status 'refunded' shows a blank screen on the order page.

The status was typed as string, and the renderer had an if/else chain without a default. Fix: a string-literal union plus an exhaustive switch with a never check, so adding a status breaks the build where it is not handled.
After upgrading to TypeScript 6, hundreds of “Cannot find name 'process'” or describe errors appear.
TS 6.0 changed types to [], so @types/node and test globals are no longer loaded automatically. Fix: list them in compilerOptions.types, e.g. ["node", "vitest/globals"].
