qs.s: type Point = { x: number; y: number }. const p3 = { x: 1, y: 2, z: 3 }; const a: Point = p3; compiles, but const b: Point = { x: 1, y: 2, z: 3 }; fails. Why?
o: The second one is a bug in TypeScript
Excess property checks only apply to fresh object literals; a variable with extra properties still fits structurally
p3 is inferred as any
const variables are not type-checked
qs.e: Structural typing allows extra properties. TypeScript adds an extra check for object literals written directly where a type is expected, because extra keys there are usually typos.

qs.s: A function gets value: string | number | null. Inside if (value) { ... }, what is its type, and what is the hidden risk?
o: string | number; risk: empty string "" and 0 are also skipped, though they may be valid values
string | number | null; the check does nothing
string; numbers are removed by truthiness
never; the branch cannot run
qs.e: Truthiness narrowing removes null, but also skips 0 and "" at runtime. For a quantity of 0, that is a real bug. Use value !== null when 0 or empty string are valid.

qs.s: An API client returns Promise<any> and the team writes const order: Order = await api.get('/orders/1'). What is true?
o: TypeScript checks that the response matches Order
It fails to compile because any is not assignable to Order
TypeScript checks it in strict mode only
It compiles with no check at all; any is assignable to everything, so a changed API shape is only found at runtime
qs.e: any silently disables checking, even in strict mode. Return unknown from the client and parse it with a schema, so mismatches fail at the boundary with a clear error.

qs.s: With default strict settings, does this compile, and what happens at runtime?

code.title: animals.ts

o: Compile error: Dog[] is not assignable to Animal[]
Compiles, then throws TypeError: dogs[1].bark is not a function, because both names point to the same array
Compile error on push, because animals is really a Dog[]
Compiles and runs fine, because TypeScript copies the array on assignment
qs.e: TypeScript treats arrays as covariant: a Dog[] can be used as an Animal[]. That is convenient but unsound when you write to it. Types are erased, so no copy happens. readonly Animal[] parameters avoid this, and noUncheckedIndexedAccess would at least force a check on dogs[1].

qs.s: Why does TypeScript report an error on the sendMail line?

code.title: notify.ts

o: Narrowing of a property does not carry into a callback, because the object could be changed before the callback runs; copy it into a const first
setTimeout callbacks are not type-checked
The if check only narrows inside the same line
email? means the type is any
qs.e: Inside the callback, TS cannot prove that user.email is still set when the timer fires, because any code could mutate user in between. Fix: const email = user.email; if (email) setTimeout(() => sendMail(email)). A const cannot be reassigned, so its narrowing survives.

qs.s: This loop fails under strict with “Element implicitly has an 'any' type because expression of type 'string' can't be used to index”. Why does Object.keys return string[] and not ('basic' | 'pro')[]?

code.title: prices.ts

o: It is a known bug that will be fixed
Object.keys only works on arrays
Because prices was declared with const
Structural typing: a value of this type may have extra keys at runtime, so claiming only 'basic' | 'pro' would be unsafe
qs.e: Any object with at least basic and pro fits the type, so the real object may have more keys. Options: Object.entries(prices) for values, a typed helper with a cast you document, or for (const k of ['basic', 'pro'] as const) when you own the key list.

qs.s: Your team wants to run .ts files directly with Node 24 (type stripping, no build step). Which tsconfig option helps most to avoid code that Node cannot run?
o: "strict": true
"isolatedDeclarations": true
"erasableSyntaxOnly": true, which reports enums, namespaces with runtime code and constructor parameter properties, because they need code generation, not just removal
"noEmit": false
qs.e: Node's type stripping only deletes type syntax; it does not transform anything. erasableSyntaxOnly (TS 5.8+) flags exactly the features that are not erasable. Replace enums with as const objects and string-literal unions. Note that Node also ignores tsconfig paths, so you still run tsc --noEmit to type-check.

interview.q: How would you model the state of a multi-step checkout in TypeScript?
answer: A discriminated union with one variant per step: { step: 'cart' } | { step: 'shipping'; cart: Cart } | { step: 'payment'; cart: Cart; address: Address } | ....
Each variant carries exactly the data that must exist in that step, so invalid combinations (payment without address) cannot be built.
Transitions are functions from one variant to the next, and rendering uses an exhaustive switch with a never check.
Data entering the machine (API, URL, storage) is parsed with a schema first; the union is for trusted internal state.
Trade-off: more types up front, but adding a step makes the compiler list every place to update; for very complex flows a state machine library (XState) can generate the same guarantees.
followups: How do you persist and restore this state safely across page reloads?
Where would you put branded types here?

interview.q: TypeScript types are erased at runtime. What does that mean for how you design an application?
answer: Nothing checks types while the code runs; as casts and any are promises, not checks.
Every trust boundary (HTTP bodies, third-party APIs, env vars, storage, queues, LLM output) needs a runtime schema, with the static type inferred from it.
Inside the boundary, rely on types and avoid repeated defensive checks.
Some TS features emit runtime code (enums, namespaces, parameter properties); prefer erasable syntax so tools like esbuild and Node type stripping work without surprises.
CI must run tsc --noEmit, because bundlers strip types without checking them.
followups: What is the difference between unknown and any in practice?
How do you type data coming from a database ORM?

interview.q: How would you move a large codebase from loose TypeScript to strict mode?
answer: Turn on strict and measure the error count; do not try to fix everything in one PR.
Enable flags one at a time (strictNullChecks gives the most value and the most errors), or use per-folder tsconfigs / a tool that tracks known errors so new code must be strict.
Fix boundaries first: typed API clients with schemas remove many downstream anys.
Ban new any with lint rules and track the count in CI so it only goes down.
Agree on team rules for as, ! and @ts-expect-error (always with a reason), and add noUncheckedIndexedAccess later for new modules.
followups: How do you stop the migration from blocking feature work?
What does TypeScript 6.0 change for a project with no explicit strict setting?

one: Generics let functions and components work over many types while keeping them connected. Conditional, mapped and template-literal types compute new types from existing ones.
an: A generic is a form with a blank you fill in once ("List of ____") and every field on the form updates to match.
how: Generics: function first<T>(xs: T[]): T | undefined. Constraints: <T extends {id: string}>.
Utility types: Partial, Pick, Omit, Record, ReturnType, Awaited, NonNullable.
Mapped types: { [K in keyof T]: ... }. Conditional types: T extends X ? A : B, with infer to extract parts.
Template literal types: `on${Capitalize<E>}` for typed event names, routes, keys.
why: Library-quality code (typed API clients, form libraries, design system props) depends on these. Seniors read them in dependencies and write the simpler ones.
trade: Type-level cleverness can make errors unreadable and slow the compiler. Prefer the simplest type that protects the caller.

myth.m: Generics are just any with extra steps.
myth.r: any disconnects types; a generic keeps input and output linked, so the compiler tracks them.

q.s: You want a function get(obj, key) whose return type matches the property type. Which signature?
o: get(obj: any, key: string): any
get<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K]
get(obj: object, key: string): unknown
get<T>(obj: T, key: string): T
q.e: K is constrained to real keys of T, and T[K] gives that property's type.

more: Variance and why function parameters are tricky
lab: Write type DeepPartial<T>, type PathKeys<T> ("a.b.c" strings), and a branded UserId.
Solve 10 problems from the type-challenges repo (easy and medium).

plain:
Generics let you write one function or component that works with many types, while keeping the connection between them. For example, “give me a list of anything, I return one item of that same thing”.

Advanced types (mapped, conditional, template literal) let you build new types from existing ones, the way functions build values from values.
bridge: You already use generics: useState<User | null>(null), Array<string>, Promise<Response>. React Query's useQuery<Data> and form libraries are built on the same tools.

walk.title: Building a typed pick helper
steps: Untyped: function pick(obj, keys) returns any. Typos in keys are not caught.
Add generics: function pick<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, keys: K[]): Pick<T, K>.
K extends keyof T means: keys must be real property names of the object.
Call pick(user, ['name', 'emial']): TypeScript flags 'emial' as an error.
The result type is exactly { name: string }, so autocomplete works on it.

terms: A type parameter like <T>, filled in when the function is used.
T extends X: T must be at least an X.
The union of an object type's property names.
A type that loops over keys: { [K in keyof T]: ... }.
A extends B ? X : Y: a type-level if/else.
insights: The goal of advanced types is a better experience for the caller, not clever code. If an error message becomes unreadable, simplify.
Read the types of libraries you use (Ctrl+click). It is the fastest way to learn these tools.
Branded types (UserId that is not just any string) prevent mixing up IDs, a real class of bugs.

prod.summary: In production, advanced types appear in shared code: typed API clients, route helpers, form libraries, design-system props and event buses. They pay off when one definition drives many call sites safely. They hurt when error messages become unreadable, editor autocomplete slows down, or CI type-checking takes minutes. Seniors keep complex types inside a few library files and give callers simple, inferred APIs.
checklist: Callers almost never write type arguments by hand; the generic is inferred from values (get(user, 'name'), not get<User, 'name'>(...)).
Complex types have type tests (expectTypeOf in Vitest, or tsd), including // @ts-expect-error lines for calls that must fail.
IDs that must not mix (UserId, OrderId) use branded types created only by a validating function.
Large unions and deep recursive types are avoided in hot shared types; type-check time is watched with tsc --extendedDiagnostics or --generateTrace.
satisfies is used for config objects so values keep their exact literal types while still being checked.
Public library types are checked against the published build (attw), not only in the source repo.
numbers: TypeScript reports “Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite” (error TS2589) when recursive types go too deep.
TypeScript 7.0's native compiler (July 2026) runs the same type system about 10x faster on large projects, but complex types still cost time.
failures: error TS2589: Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite after adding a deep-path helper type.
A recursive type (PathKeys<T>) walks a large or recursive object type without a depth limit. Fix: add a depth counter to the recursion, or type only the paths you really use.
CI typecheck time grows from 40s to 6 minutes; editor hover takes seconds.

A huge union (thousands of template-literal combinations) or a deeply generic ORM type is used in many files. Fix: find hot spots with tsc --generateTrace, simplify the type, add explicit return-type annotations on exported functions.
A payment is sent to the wrong customer: refund(orderId, userId) was called with arguments swapped and type-checked fine.
Both parameters were plain string. Fix: branded types (string & { readonly __brand: 'UserId' }) so swapping is a compile error.
Developers copy-paste as unknown as T to make a typed helper compile.

The generic signature does not express the real relationship, so callers fight it. Fix: redesign the signature (constraints, overloads) or simplify; a cast inside one well-tested helper is fine, casts at every call site are not.

qs.s: type ToArray<T> = T extends unknown ? T[] : never; What is ToArray<string | number>?
o: (string | number)[]
string[] | number[]
never
unknown[]
qs.e: Conditional types distribute over unions when the checked type is a naked type parameter. To get (string | number)[], wrap it: [T] extends [unknown] ? T[] : never.

qs.s: A theme config is written as const theme: Record<string, string> = { primary: '#000' }. Now theme.primry (typo) compiles. What fixes it while still checking every value is a string?
o: Use as const only
Use any
Write const theme = { primary: '#000' } satisfies Record<string, string>
Use Partial<Record<string, string>>
qs.e: satisfies checks the value against the type but keeps the narrower inferred type, so only real keys exist. A type annotation widens it to “any string key”. as const alone keeps the keys but does not check the values.

qs.s: Your shared DeepPaths<T> type makes the editor freeze on a large Prisma model and CI shows TS2589. Best senior response?
o: Limit recursion depth or type only the paths you need, and measure with tsc --generateTrace
Increase Node memory for tsc
Replace the type with any everywhere it is used
Turn off strict mode
qs.e: The type is too expensive by design. Limiting it keeps most safety. More memory does not fix a depth limit; any throws away the safety completely; strict has nothing to do with it.

o: Compile error: 'iddle' is not one of the states
Runtime error
Compile error: S cannot be inferred
It compiles: S is inferred from both arguments as 'idle' | 'loading' | 'done' | 'iddle'. Write initial: NoInfer<S> (TS 5.4+) so only states drives inference
qs.e: TypeScript collects inference candidates for S from every argument, so the typo becomes part of the union. NoInfer<S> tells the compiler not to infer from that position, and then 'iddle' is reported. Before 5.4 the trick was a second type parameter I extends S.

o: { getName: () => string; getAge: () => number }
{ name: () => string; age: () => number }
{ getname: () => string; getage: () => number }
never, because template literals cannot be used as keys
qs.e: The as clause remaps each key: Capitalize turns name into Name, giving getName. string & K drops number and symbol keys, which cannot go into a template literal. Key remapping can also filter: mapping a key to never removes it.

qs.s: With strictFunctionTypes on, only one of these assignments is an error. Which, and why?

code.title: handlers.ts

o: Both are errors
Only b is an error: parameters of method-syntax members are still checked bivariantly, function-type properties contravariantly
Only a is an error: methods are checked more strictly than properties
Neither; parameter types are never checked
qs.e: Both are unsafe: a KeyboardEvent could reach code that reads clientX. strictFunctionTypes applies only to function-type properties; method syntax stays bivariant for compatibility (e.g. with DOM types and arrays). If you want the stricter check in your own interfaces, declare callbacks as properties.

qs.s: getUser(id, { withOrders: true }) should return UserWithOrders, and without the flag a plain User. Which approach gives callers correct types with the least risk?
o: Return User | UserWithOrders and let callers check
Two overload signatures (one with { withOrders: true }, one without) above one implementation
A generic with a conditional return type W extends true ? UserWithOrders : User, casting inside the implementation
Return any
qs.e: Overloads read like documentation and are easy for callers. A conditional return type also works, but TypeScript cannot check the implementation against it, so you need a cast, and a caller passing a plain boolean gets a union anyway. A union return pushes the check onto every caller. Often the best option is two functions (getUser, getUserWithOrders).

interview.q: When do you use generics, and when are they overkill?
answer: Use a generic when it connects types: input to output (first<T>(xs: T[]): T | undefined), or two parameters to each other (K extends keyof T).
If a type parameter appears only once in the signature, it adds nothing; use the concrete type or unknown.
Callers should almost never write type arguments; if they must, inference is not working and the signature should change.
Constraints (extends) document what the function needs; NoInfer controls which argument drives inference.
Keep complex generics in a few shared modules with type tests (expectTypeOf, @ts-expect-error).
followups: What is the difference between a generic and a union parameter?
How do you test types?

interview.q: Explain conditional types with infer. Show a real use case.
answer: T extends X ? A : B is an if/else on types; infer captures a part of the matched type, like a regex group.
Built-ins use it: ReturnType, Parameters, Awaited.
Real use: extracting route params from a string such as '/users/:id' with template-literal infer, or the element type of an API response wrapper.
They distribute over unions when the checked type is a bare type parameter; wrap it in [T] to stop that.
Costs: recursion limits (TS2589), slow checking and unreadable errors; set depth limits and keep them out of hot shared types.
followups: Why does ToArray<string | number> give string[] | number[]?
How would you debug a slow type?

interview.q: How do you keep type-level code maintainable and fast in a large codebase?
answer: Prefer simple types that callers understand; put any clever type behind a small API in one module.
Add explicit return types to exported functions, which stops expensive inference from spreading and gives faster, clearer errors.

Review type complexity like code complexity: if the error message is unreadable to a teammate, simplify.

one: Parse untrusted data (requests, API responses, env vars, localStorage, LLM output) with a schema at the edge of your system, and get typed data or a clear error.
an: Customs at the border. Inside the country everyone trusts passports have been checked, because they were checked once, at the border.
how: Libraries: Zod (v4), Valibot, ArkType, Yup. Define a schema once, infer the TS type from it: type User = z.infer<typeof User>. Many frameworks accept any of them through the shared Standard Schema interface.
"Parse, don't validate": User.parse(json) returns typed, cleaned data (coerced, defaults applied, unknown keys stripped) or throws. safeParse returns { success, data | error } instead of throwing.
Use at every trust boundary: API handlers, form submissions, third-party responses, env config, messages from queues, and JSON produced by an LLM.
Share schemas between frontend and backend in a monorepo for one source of truth.
why: TypeScript cannot see runtime data. Validation at the boundary is what makes the types inside honest, and it is a security control (mass assignment, injection).
trade: Validation costs some CPU on very hot paths and schema duplication if not shared. Generated schemas from OpenAPI can help.

myth.r: Frontend validation is UX. Anyone can call your API directly, so the server must validate too.

q.s: An endpoint does const body = req.body as UpdateUser and passes it to db.update. A user adds isAdmin: true to the JSON. What happens and why?
o: Nothing; TS removes isAdmin
It may be written to the DB (mass assignment); 'as' is not a runtime check
TS throws at runtime
The DB rejects it automatically
q.e: Parse with a strict schema that allows only the editable fields.

plain:
TypeScript cannot see data that arrives while the app runs: API responses, form input, URL parameters, environment variables, AI output. Any of these can be wrong.

So at the edge of your system, you check the data against a schema. If it matches, you get typed, clean data. If not, you get a clear error and stop. Inside your system you can then trust the types.
bridge: You have probably written const user = await res.json() as User. The as is a promise to the compiler, not a check. If the API changes, your app crashes deep inside a component instead of failing clearly at the fetch.

walk.title: Protecting a profile update endpoint
steps: Define a schema: const UpdateProfile = z.object({ name: z.string().min(1).max(80), bio: z.string().max(500).optional() }).
Get the type for free: type UpdateProfile = z.infer<typeof UpdateProfile>.
In the handler: const result = UpdateProfile.safeParse(req.body). If result.success is false, return 422 with the field errors.

A user sends extra fields like isAdmin: true. z.object strips unknown keys from result.data, so pass result.data to the database, never req.body. (Use z.strictObject if you want to reject the request instead.)
Use the same schema in the React form for instant feedback, so frontend and backend rules never drift apart.

terms: A description of what valid data looks like, checked at runtime.
Check data and return a cleaned, typed version, or an error.
The point where data comes from outside your control.
A bug where extra fields in a request (like isAdmin) get saved because nothing filtered them.
insights: Validate once at the boundary, then trust the types inside. Do not sprinkle checks everywhere.
Parsing also normalises: trimming, turning "42" into 42 and applying defaults happen once, at the edge, so inner code never repeats them.
LLM output is untrusted input too. Parse it with a schema before using it.

prod.summary: In production, validation is where bad input becomes a clean 400/422 with field errors instead of a 500 deep inside the code, a corrupted database row, or a security hole. Seniors validate every request body, query string, env variable, webhook and third-party response at the edge, decide what happens to unknown keys, and log validation failures from partners as an alert signal.
checklist: Every route parses body, params and query with a schema before any business logic; nothing uses req.body as X.
Update endpoints use an explicit allow-list schema (only editable fields). Use z.strictObject to reject unknown keys when clients should never send them; the default z.object strips them.
Environment variables are parsed once at startup; a missing DATABASE_URL stops the process with a clear message, not a crash at the first query.
Strings have max lengths and arrays have max sizes, so a 10MB string or 1M-element array is rejected early (also set a body-size limit on the server).
Validation errors return 400 or 422 with field paths (e.g. z.flattenError(err)), and never echo stack traces.
Third-party responses and webhooks are parsed too; failures are logged with the partner name and counted, because they mean the contract changed.
LLM JSON output is parsed with the same schema; on failure retry once or fall back, never pass it on unchecked.
numbers: Zod 4: z.object strips unknown keys by default; z.strictObject rejects them; z.looseObject passes them through.
Zod 4 error helpers: z.flattenError (flat fieldErrors for forms), z.treeifyError (nested), z.prettifyError (readable string); z.formatError is deprecated.
Express express.json() default body limit is 100kb; requests above it get 413.
failures: A normal user becomes admin after editing their profile.

The handler spread req.body into the update (db.user.update({ data: req.body })), so role: 'admin' was saved (mass assignment). Fix: parse with a schema that lists only editable fields; consider z.strictObject to reject extra keys and log the attempt.
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'amount') deep in billing code after a partner API release.

The partner renamed a field; the response was cast with as, so the error appeared far from the cause. Fix: safeParse the response at the client, raise a clear “partner contract changed” error, and alert on it.
Service starts, passes health checks, then fails the first payment with “invalid API key”.
process.env.STRIPE_KEY was undefined in the new environment. Fix: validate all env vars with a schema at boot so the deploy fails immediately.
A search endpoint is slow and memory spikes when someone sends ?ids= with 200,000 values.
No size limits in the schema. Fix: z.array(z.uuid()).max(100) (Zod 4 top-level form; z.string().uuid() is deprecated), string .max() limits, and a body/query size limit at the server.

qs.s: A Zod 4 schema z.object({ name: z.string() }) parses { "name": "Ann", "isAdmin": true }. What does parse return?
o: It throws because isAdmin is unknown
{ name: 'Ann' }: unknown keys are stripped by default
{ name: 'Ann', isAdmin: true }
{ name: 'Ann', isAdmin: undefined }
qs.e: z.object strips unknown keys. To throw instead, use z.strictObject; to keep them, z.looseObject. Stripping protects you only if you use the parsed result, not the original req.body.

qs.s: A handler does const r = Body.safeParse(req.body); if (!r.success) return res.status(422).end(); await db.order.create({ data: req.body });. Is it safe?
o: Yes, the body was validated
Yes, if the schema is strict
No, safeParse does not check types
No: it validates but then saves the original req.body, so stripped or coerced values are ignored; use r.data
qs.e: “Parse, don't validate”: the result of parsing is the trusted value. With the default strip mode, extra keys are still in req.body. A strict schema would reject extra keys, but coercions and defaults would still be lost.

qs.s: ?page=2 reaches your handler. Schema: z.object({ page: z.number().int().min(1) }). Every request fails validation. Why?
o: Query string values are strings; use z.coerce.number() for query and env values
Zod cannot validate query strings
min(1) rejects 2
int() only accepts bigint
qs.e: URLs and env vars only carry strings, so "2" is not a number. z.coerce.number() converts first. Be careful: coercion turns "" into 0, so keep .min(1).

qs.s: What does the last line do with Zod 4?

code.title: query.ts

o: Returns { limit: 100, sort: 'new' }: max() clamps the value
Returns { limit: 20, sort: 'new' }: the default replaces invalid values
Throws a ZodError: '500' is coerced to 500, which fails max(100)
Returns { limit: '500', sort: 'new' }: coercion only happens for env vars
qs.e: Checks like .max() reject; they never change the value. Defaults apply only when the input is undefined, not when it is invalid. If you want clamping, add it explicitly with .transform(), but usually a 400/422 with a clear message is better for an API.

qs.s: A Stripe-style webhook handler rejects every real event with “signature mismatch”. What is wrong?

code.title: webhook.ts

o: The schema must be strict

The signature is computed over the exact raw bytes; re-stringifying parsed JSON changes whitespace and key order. Read the raw body (express.raw for this route), verify first, then parse with the schema
res.sendStatus must be called before verification
JSON.stringify should use 2-space indentation
qs.e: Webhook signatures are HMACs of the raw request body. Any change, even a space, breaks them. Order matters too: authenticate (verify the signature), then validate the shape. Parsing untrusted data before verifying also means you do schema work for forged requests.

qs.s: .env contains FEATURE_X=false. The schema is z.object({ FEATURE_X: z.coerce.boolean().default(false) }). What is env.FEATURE_X?
o: false
undefined
A ZodError, because “false” is not a boolean
true: coerce.boolean uses JavaScript truthiness, and any non-empty string, including “false”, is truthy. Use z.stringbool() in Zod 4
qs.e: z.coerce.boolean() is Boolean(input). Boolean('false') and Boolean('0') are both true. Zod 4's z.stringbool() understands “true/false”, “1/0”, “yes/no”, “on/off”. This bug has turned on features in production that were meant to be off.

qs.s: A payment partner adds a new optional field and a new status value 'partially_refunded'. Your client parses their responses with z.strictObject and a closed z.enum. Now every response fails and checkout is down. What policy fits third-party responses best?
o: Accept unknown keys (default strip mode), handle unknown enum values with a fallback branch, and alert when unknown values appear; stay strict on the fields you actually use
Keep everything strict; outages force partners to communicate changes
Stop validating partner responses and cast them with as
Validate only in tests, not in production
qs.e: Be strict about what you send and what you depend on, tolerant about additions you do not use. A closed enum on a field that grows over time turns a harmless partner release into your outage. Removing validation brings back the crash-deep-inside problem. Logging unknown values tells you to update the code without breaking users.

interview.q: Where are the trust boundaries in a typical web app, and how do you validate at each?
answer: Incoming HTTP: body, params, query and headers parsed with a schema before business logic; 400/422 with field errors; size limits on strings, arrays and body.
Outgoing calls: third-party and internal-service responses parsed at the client, with failures logged by partner and alerted on.
Configuration: env vars parsed once at startup so a bad deploy fails immediately.
Async inputs: queue messages, webhooks (verify signature on the raw body first), files, localStorage, and LLM output.
After parsing, pass only the parsed value inward; never re-use the raw input.

interview.q: How do you keep one source of truth for data shapes between frontend and backend?
answer: In a TypeScript monorepo: share schemas in a package and infer types with z.infer; the form and the handler use the same rules.
Across languages or teams: an OpenAPI or JSON Schema contract as the source, with generated clients and validators, checked in CI.
Version the contract: additive changes are safe; removals and renames need a deprecation period.
Frontend validation is UX only; the server always validates again with the same or stricter rules.
Contract tests or schema diff checks in CI catch breaking changes before deploy.

interview.q: How strict should validation be for requests you receive versus responses you consume?
answer: Requests to your API: strict. Allow-list editable fields, consider rejecting unknown keys on sensitive endpoints, enforce sizes and formats; it is a security control (mass assignment, injection, DoS).
Responses from others: tolerant of additions, strict on what you use. Strip unknown keys and give unknown enum values a fallback.
Decide per field what failure means: reject the request, drop the item, or use a default, and log which one happened.
Watch validation failure rates as a metric; a spike from one partner or one client version is an early warning of a contract change.
Never echo internal details in error responses; return field paths and messages only.
